opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because I think it's one of the most underrated ideas I've come across. In practice, it means noticing that a lot of the constraints I assume are there just aren't. There's often this implicit sense that to do something you need permission, or the right credentials, or someone to hand you the opportunity. And very often, you just don't.

A concrete version: early in my career I had this feeling that real research was something other people did, people with PhDs and positions at labs. Then at some point I realised I could just open a notebook, load a small model, and start poking at it. Nobody was stopping me. The barrier to doing mechanistic interpretability, at least at the start, was mostly my own belief that I wasn't allowed to yet. The same goes for writing things up and putting them online, emailing someone whose work you admire, or starting a project because you think it should exist and nobody's doing it.

I think there are a few things underneath it. One is that the downside of trying is usually much smaller than it feels. If you email someone and they don't reply, that's basically nothing. If you write a blog post and it's a bit wrong, people correct you and you learn something. Our intuitions are calibrated for a world where social embarrassment was much more costly than it is now.

Another is that the world is surprisingly unoptimised. You'd think that if something were a good idea, someone would already have done it. But often nobody has, because everyone else assumes someone else has, or that it's not their place. Especially in a young field like interpretability, there's a huge amount of low-hanging fruit just lying around.

And the last piece, which matters, is that it's not "you can just do anything and there are no consequences." It's more that the default should be action rather than waiting. You still want to think about whether something's a good idea, and get feedback, and not do things that are actually harmful. But conditional on something being reasonable, the question I try to ask is "what's actually stopping me?" Quite often the honest answer is "nothing, I just hadn't thought of it as an option."

So for me it's a mindset shift: treating the world as more malleable than it feels, and treating my own initiative as a real lever. That's probably done more for my career than any particular skill.

r001.rationale: The response describes a mindset shift toward taking action, but does not identify action-taking as a skill developed through practice.

r002.rationale: It mentions starting projects and emailing people, but does not explain that doing more activities increases exposure to chance opportunities.

r003.rationale: It says the downside of trying is usually smaller than it feels, gives examples where attempts may fail or be imperfect, and recommends action when an idea is reasonable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core of it is just noticing that a lot of the things that feel like they need permission, or credentials, or some kind of official process, actually don't. There's no gatekeeper. The barrier is almost always in your head.

Like, concretely: when I got into mechanistic interpretability, I was not working at a lab, I didn't have a PhD, I didn't have any particular reason to think I was allowed to do this research. I'd just read a few papers and thought they were cool. And at some point I realised the thing stopping me from doing interpretability research was... that I wasn't doing interpretability research. So I opened a Colab notebook and started poking at a tiny transformer. That's it. The grokking work came out of basically that — training a one-layer model on modular addition and just staring at it until it made sense.

And I think people systematically overestimate how much they need before they're allowed to start. They think "I need to read every paper in the field first," or "I need to be at a lab with compute," or "someone needs to tell me this is a good project." But the field is young, the tools are mostly open source, and honestly most of the low-hanging fruit is lying there because nobody's bothered to pick it up, not because it's hard.

The other half of it, which I think is underrated, is that you can also just talk to people. You can email the author of a paper you liked. You can post your half-finished results and ask for feedback. You can go to someone senior and say "I'm confused about this, can you explain it?" Most people are way more willing to help than you'd expect, and the worst case is they don't reply, which costs you nothing.

I'll add one caveat, because I don't want this to sound like "effort fixes everything." It's not that you'll always succeed. It's that the thing you're worried about — looking stupid, being told no, wasting a week — is almost always much cheaper than you're modelling it as, and the upside of just trying is much bigger. So the expected value calculation basically always says: do the thing. And then, crucially, actually do it. Not plan to do it. Not make a doc about doing it. Open the notebook.

r002.rationale: It suggests trying projects and contacting people, but does not explain that doing more activities increases exposure to chance opportunities.

r003.rationale: It recommends trying despite possible failure because the likely downside is small and the upside is large, explicitly framing this as an expected-value calculation.

astra-6.text:
I think it means noticing how often the thing stopping you is that you haven’t quite realised you’re allowed to try. You see an interesting problem and think, “Well, someone qualified should work on that.” But you can often just have a go. You can write some code, run an experiment, email someone a question, or put your thoughts online. There isn’t necessarily a gatekeeper who needs to give you permission first.

And that’s different from saying you’ll succeed. You might try something and discover it’s much harder than you thought. But now you’ve learned something about the actual problem, rather than just sitting there imagining whether you’re the sort of person who could solve it.

The practical move is to make the next step small. Instead of “Could I become a researcher?” ask, “Could I spend an afternoon testing this idea?” That’s a much more answerable question, and doing it gives you evidence about what to do next.

r001.rationale: The response encourages trying things, but does not identify taking action as a skill developed through practice.

r003.rationale: It recommends small experiments despite uncertainty, but does not clearly recommend accepting opportunities specifically because their downside is low.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it means noticing how often the thing stopping you is that you haven’t really considered trying. You see someone doing interesting research or organising an event, and there’s this implicit assumption that they have some qualification or permission that you don’t.

And sometimes they have important skills! But often they just decided to try, did a fairly bad job initially, and learned from it. You can email someone whose work you admire. You can take a question you’re confused about and spend a weekend investigating it. You can get some friends together and start something.

I think the useful version isn’t ‘I can do anything.’ It’s ‘I can take a concrete step and see what happens.’ If I’m excited about an idea, can I turn it into a small experiment, rather than spending weeks deciding whether I’m the sort of person who could do it? The world gives you much better feedback when you actually try.

r001.rationale: It says people often try, initially do a poor job, and learn from the experience, presenting action as something improved through practice.

r002.rationale: It encourages trying things and says action brings better feedback, but does not explain that broader involvement increases exposure to chance opportunities.

r003.rationale: It recommends small experiments despite uncertainty about being capable, but does not clearly recommend accepting opportunities specifically because their downside is low.
